segments.text: Hi everybody and welcome to this week's
edition of Central Florida Spotlight.
I'm Greg Warmoth. We recently sat down,
as you know, with Democratic candidate
for governor David Jolly. And today,
Republican nominee Congressman Byron
Donalds joins us to discuss his plans
and respond to what Jolly told us. And
Congressman is actually on a bus right
now as he continues to get out the vote,
and this is this is our first for us,
Congressman Donalds. We've never
interviewed anyone before on a bus.
Thank you.
>> Well, look it's pleasure to be with you.
You know, first time for everything but
I look forward to the conversation.
>> So, what is the strongest reason that a
Central Florida voter should choose you
and what would you actually change in
that voter's daily life here in Central
Florida because it seems like sometimes
we're forgotten even though we're this
huge city.
>> Well, first and foremost Florida is the
best state in America. Everybody knows
this. It's not a it's not something that
gets debated. We have people who've
chosen to live in Florida. They come
here from every part of America and the
reason why is because we're a common
sense state that stands by just common
sense principles, conservative
principles. We back law enforcement in
our state. We make sure parents are the
ones who are making decisions on behalf
of their children when it comes to
education. We have an incredibly great
quality of life. We just really embody
just a limited government that largely
lets people live their lives. That's the
recipe for success that has made Florida
number one.
As governor, what I would do is be
focused on the affordability issues that
are hurting Floridians in our state. We
have to lower insurance costs. My plan
will lower them 20%for Floridians. We
want to make sure that people can
actually be able to get the housing that
they need. We have to lower the cost of
construction. This is why I'm laser
focused on permitting reform to lower
the cost of construction in our state.
We also want to make sure there's enough
ways for sick days. That's going I'm a
graduate of Florida State University. Uh
but that you you don't have to be in the
university system to be successful. We
want our kids in high school to be able
to get access to internships or
apprenticeships if they're not going to
go to the university system. It's all
about making sure Florida remains the
best state in America and that's why I'm
running for governor.
>> There have been um
predecessors who have not accepted um
and Rick Scott comes to mind Medicare
assistance or Medicaid assistance. Would
you take money from the federal
government?
>> Uh no, Medicaid expansion has actually
not been working. Uh, initially what it
did, it provided more money. But what
Medicaid expansion does is you're
providing Medicaid to able-bodied adults
between the ages of 18 and 55, and
you're doing it, um, at a higher cost
than you would poor people, poor
elderly, poor children, which is the
real purpose of Medicaid. And so what we
want to be focused on is price
transparency, not just at the front door
when people walk in, but also the
payment system of healthcare so we can
have efficiencies in that to lower costs
and stabilize costs. I believe that's
the better way to go. And let's be also
be very clear: if Florida had expanded
Medicaid a couple of years ago,
Florida's budget would have been
significantly higher, our debt levels
would have been significantly higher,
and we would be struggling to actually
have resources for education, for water
projects, and some of the other
essential services that the state of
Florida has to provide for its people.
>> Transportation, do you support
high-speed rail, anything like that to
get us off I-4 so we can get to Tampa?
Would you help?
>> when it comes to high-speed rail, it's
always going to be about how many people
are going to ride it and how and and how
long do you have to subsidize it?
Because if you have to subsidize it uh
over an extended period of time, that
takes resources away from the
conversation we were just having around
healthcare, especially for those who are
poor, who do need help. And what about
when it comes to the future of education
in our state? How do we provide more
dollars into education? So uh before we
get into a high-speed rail conversation,
I want to make sure that the math works.
If the math works, that's something
we'll support. If the math does not
work, uh you'd be hard-pressed to sup-
for me to find me to support it because
what will happen is we'll have to
constantly subsidize it. I do believe my
permitting agenda, that will actually
help uh infrastructure, especially road
infrastructure, to build out the roads
that we need to alleviate traffic on the
I-4 corridor.
>> We're going to come right back with our
continuing conversation with Congressman
Byron Donalds, who in a few days could
be the new governor of Florida. That's
up next.
Welcome back to Central Florida
Spotlight. We're back with Byron Donalds
in our interview with David Jolly. He
repeatedly challenged the accuracy of
your campaign uh a negative ad. Jolly,
uh according to again the publication
that's come out from your your team, to
raise taxes on tips, overtime, and
Social Security. He calls that a lie.
What is the truth there?
>> The truth is that David Jolly, when he
was a commentator on MSNBC, he said that
he actually did not support what we
pushed through last year on Capitol
Hill, which cut taxes for working
families all across Florida. It also
made sure that we kept small business
taxes low for Floridians. David Jolly
said that that should be undone. So,
what we're saying is true even though he
doesn't want to admit it.
>> Also, an ad says that Jolly would bring
higher property taxes, higher insurance
costs, socialism. Are there some
specific policies that you're calling
socialist with Mr. Jolly?
>> Anytime you have a government takeover
of insurance or any industry, that is
socialism. That's number one. His
insurance plan is a complete takeover by
the state of Florida of wind insurance.
And anytime we've seen the government
takeover any industry, it never works.
And the actually the prices get higher
for people and the services get worse.
That's why you can't have governments
takeover something like insurance. When
When to higher property taxes, he
opposes Amendment 3. He doesn't talk
about solutions to drive actually give
Floridians the relief that they so
richly deserve. He won't lift a finger
to do any of that. And so, that's why
our critiques of Mr. Jolly are accurate.
He can just call them a lie, but he
won't debate these issues with me. He
has run from the debates. I challenged
him to to three. He said no, because he
doesn't want to have to answer questions
in front of the people of Florida.
>> Social media had um somebody I don't
know if if it was staged or whatever,
but um
they wanted you to call a person a man
and you had said sir and that kind of
ties into my next question. First of
all, I don't know if you want to respond
to that that moment um how you stood
face to face.
>> I mean, there's nothing to respond to.
By the way, that was something that was
released by one of the protesters, not
my campaign. We actually took the
footage of that event because we went
over to actually talk to the protesters
that were at my event in Pasco County.
Uh we like to record those events
because if somebody tries to splice the
video or something then you have the
backup and you can respond with the
truth. Uh we saw that one of the
protesters released that video and it's
really taken on a life of its own on
social media. So, really there's nothing
to respond to.
>> Okay, so let's dovetail into this. Jolly
again sat here told me he would not
change Florida's current transgender
sports law. Do you accept that
commitment? Um because again it was one
of those situations where he called you
literally on this TV station a liar when
it comes to that.
>> Well, David Jolly by his own words has
said that he supports boys and girls
sports. He said that, not me. We
actually take his words. And so, again,
if he felt so strongly about my
critique, then he should have debated
me, but he chose not to. He chose to run
from the voters of Florida. But it's
bigger than that. Let's be Let's be
honest about where the Democrat Party is
today. This is not the Democrat Party of
Bill Clinton. It's not even the Democrat
Party of JFK. This is now the Democrat
Party of Bernie Sanders and
Ocasio-Cortez and the radicals in the
Democrat Socialists of America. And so
he can say whatever he wants today, but
when you actually have to bring staff
into an administration like our State
Department of Education or the trustees
system at our universities or the Board
of Governors, who's he going to go to
for that? The same people who use common
sense that have made Florida's
university system the number one system
in all of America or are you going to
use people from the Democrat Party to
staff these positions? Cuz let's be very
clear: even though he showed up a year
ago to become a Democrat, the Democrats
long standing in that party, they're
going to want to be sitting in these
seats of authority and power all across
Florida. And that will turn our state
into just another blue state or purple
state, like we've seen all across the
country that the people of Central
Florida and the people of Florida
overall have escaped from, and they've
come to Florida.
>> Jolly, one more uh thing that he had a
real problem with. He said um
he is not support uh supporting offshore
oil drilling and he said his
congressional record backs that. First
of all, if you could um address his
claims that that's a lie and and where
where do you stand on
um new oil drilling off Florida's coast?
>> Well, as I I've always been against oil
drilling off the coast of Florida. I've
never supported it at any given point in
time. Uh David Jolly can talk about his
record in Congress, but when he was a
lobbyist in Washington, he lobbied for
oil drilling. That's a fact. We've
documented that.
>> All right, next up with again on the
road literally. I mean, play the Willie
Nelson song because he is on the road on
a bus talking to us. We appreciate it.
Next, data centers, electricity bills
and property taxes, who benefits and who
pays? We continue with Congressman Byron
Donalds next.
Welcome back to Central Florida
Spotlight. Central Florida's growth is
bringing questions about electricity,
water, housing, and the cost of local
services. Again, we bring back in Byron
Donalds, congressman running for Florida
governor, and we'll know just in a few
days whether or not he is successful.
Let's talk about
He said he would impose a day one
moratorium on hyperscale data centers.
He feels like that's a way to beat you.
If you could clear the air on data
centers and your stance.
>> Of course. A state law today signed by
Governor DeSantis, and by the way, my
running mate, Brian Avila, was the
author of the legislation. It's very
clear when it comes to data centers.
First and foremost, only local
communities will be making these
decisions. If a community says no data
centers, then no data centers. As
governor, we will not preempt local
governments. They are the ones that
issue building permits. If a local
government says no, if a community says
no, then there's going to be no data
centers, period. Number two, if a
community does say they want to build
one of these, then state protections
under current law go into effect. Number
one, we're not going to see utility
bills rise on the people of Florida for
a hyperscale data center. It is against
Florida's law for a consumer to have to
pay those bills. Number two, our our
laws today call for use permits,
water use permits for a data center.
Florida's been issuing use permits for
decades. We do this to protect our
aquifers. As governor, my responsibility
to protect our aquifers and to protect
our environment, because if we don't
have a thriving environment, we're not
going to have a thriving economy here in
the Sunshine State. The two actually
work hand in hand. Number three, the
David Jolly says he wants a moratorium
that so he can study it. Well, here's
the problem. If you're going to run for
governor, you should actually know the
laws of our state. Because in the bill
that my running mate was the author for,
that Governor DeSantis has now signed
into law, that we're going to keep as
law in under my term as governor, it's
very clear that the state has already
issued, actually um, commissioned a
study. That study's due back June 1 of
2027. So, the study that David Jolly
says he's looking for, the state of
Florida under Republican leadership has
already commissioned that study. We're
going to release the findings to the
people of Florida, to all local
governments, so that everybody has the
key information about what the impacts
are with respect to data centers. I
think to the people who want to
criticize me, they say that I'm going to
build data centers all over the place.
Well, that's a flat-out lie. Number one,
governors don't issue building permits,
local governments do. Number two, we're
not going to build data centers in
communities that do not want them. The
thing that I think I think Jolly went up
to Virginia to look at Data Center
Alley. What they did in Northern
Virginia, we are not going to do in
Florida. I believe if they do get built,
you have to keep them away from
residential areas. Nobody wants them
next to their home. I don't want them
next to my home. And so, we want to make
sure that they're away. The last piece,
I think if there's anything I would
change in the current state law, it's
around transparency. I do think if a if
a project wants to come to a community,
they should be transparent with the
people in that in that community and
have an open dialogue about what are the
opportunities, what are the things that
have to get mitigated, and what are the
threats, so local communities can make
those decisions. That is my position
when it comes to data centers.
>> He said we should be concerned that
you've received millions of dollars from
data center interests. Is that accurate?
>> No, because no matter who's supported my
campaign, the policies that I have put
forward, the policies I support have
always been about what's in the best
interest of Florida, Florida's people,
Florida's economy, and Florida's
environment. And as governor, that is
exactly what I'm going to continue to
do. And to be very clear, yes, we've
been blessed to have a lot of support in
this campaign, but I've not promised any
policy to any interest. We always talk
about the same policies that I've been
campaigning on are the same policies
that we will execute as the state's next
governor.
>> One more thing that he referenced here,
Amendment 3. You guys are
on opposite ends of this argument.
You're going to vote yes, he's going to
vote no for Amendment 3. Let's say it's
a yes. He believes it leaves rural
counties um really susceptible to try to
find um money to fund public safety. How
much does a homeowner uh need to be
concerned if it passes that some of
their safety measures won't be there
when they call 911?
>> Well, once again, if you're going to run
for governor, you should actually do
your homework. And David Jolly's not
done any homework. He just wants to
point fingers and complain. Listen, I
support Amendment 3 because property
taxes in our state have gone from $32
billion
about 6 years ago to almost $56 billion
today. They're projected to go to to
over $80 billion in a couple of years.
The people of Florida are not a
never-ending piggy bank for government.
They do deserve relief. And I think
local governments had a responsibility
over the last several years to do what's
called a rollback rate, so they can
smooth out property tax collections,
being mindful of the super high
inflation from the Biden years and the
Biden economy and to making sure that
the people have enough money in their
pocket to make ends meet. When it comes
to rural communities, Governor DeSantis
said this: "When Amendment 3 came up
there in the legislature, and I've made
the further commitment that for for
rural counties, we're going to set up a
funding formula so those counties get
the resources that they need in order to
keep law enforcement in place and to
keep their communities from a local
government perspective intact." I think
that's important. The state of Florida
can step up and help those rural commit
uh communities. The The last thing I
will say, if Amendment 3 passes or even
if Amendment 3 fails, we're going to
bring this back into Florida's Tax and
Budget Reform Commission. That
commission gets at next year. We do want
to repeal homestead property taxes, but
if we can't make that math work, we want
to target the relief to seniors on fixed
income and working families. So, that's
why I support Amendment 3. That's how
we'll continue to help local
communities, especially rural
communities. And we do have a plan of
actually using the state's commission,
which is in our Constitution, to help
Floridians across the board when it
comes to making ends meet on lower
property taxes in our state while making
sure our public safety officials get the
funding they they need and so do local
governments.
>> All right, when we return health care,
schools, and whether or not Governor
Donalds would be willing to tell
President Donald Trump no. That's next.
Welcome back to our final segment with
Byron Donalds, congressman running to be
your next governor here in Florida. In a
few days we'll know if it's a yes or no.
And I want to first of all, again, for
those who are just joining us, um
Congressman Donalds is riding on his bus
as he continues to campaign tirelessly.
If there were 24 hours in a day that he
could use awake and campaigning, I I
feel like I don't know if you would say
yes, but your team would because we are
approaching the finish line. How are you
doing in terms of uh the fuel in your
body to keep going to that finish line?
>> Well, I got to tell you we it's been a
great campaign. We've been all over
Florida. Um, yeah, sometimes you might
get a little fatigued, but when you talk
to the the the Floridians, when you talk
to people, when you engage them
directly, you hear what their concerns
are from them, and you talk about how
you can help fix it and how you can make
life better in our state. That's what
gives you energy. So, we we're doing
maybe five or six events a day. Uh
that's been consistent now for the past
really 6 months or so and we're really
excited about the prospects of November
3rd. But, that's how we keep the energy
level up. We just go see the people of
Florida. Um they really do love this
state and I think that's a non-partisan
statement. It doesn't matter.
Republican, independent, Democrat, uh
we've met voters from all walks of life,
from all political parties. The one
thing that has united the people of our
state consistently, they love Florida.
>> So, I want to leave um with another one
of his ads. Jolly had an ad where he
says
um or they use your comment "Daddy's
back" and your A grade for President
Trump's economy to argue that your
loyalty comes before Floridians'
financial interest. I want to leave you
with the opportunity to respond to that
here on Channel 9.
>> Uh first of all, David Jolly's ad is
ridiculous. Um at those times I've
disagreed with President Trump. When it
comes to AI, the president wants a
federal framework for AI. I think
Florida should lead. I told the
president very directly, I think this is
what we should be doing. When it be we
should be doing it at the state level,
not the federal level. When it comes to
right now, the federal government and
the Senate, they moved this bill to save
college sports. I actually disagree with
that bill. I think we should let the
current system continue to be in place.
These players using their name, image,
and likeness, I think that's a good
thing. It's nothing wrong with people
being able to use their talents and
their abilities and their or their fame
to be able to make money. That That's
America. And I do support that. If
you're going to talk about the economy,
I think the moves that the president
made coming in have actually helped the
economy overall. But we are people are
having to deal with higher gas prices,
higher energy prices. But that's not
economic policy. That's actually a
foreign policy issue, not an economic
policy issue. If you want to look deeper
into energy policy in our country, the
things that has made it harder for us to
have cheaper and affordable energy is
actually Democrat policy around the
Green New Scam, where they favor solar
panels over natural gas, where they
actually stop you from having the
pipeline infrastructure you need to get
cheaper fuel to more places to lower
those costs. I think um if you take a
look at oil refineries, then the United
States of America has not built a new
oil refinery in 50 years. But our demand
for petroleum, our demand for gasoline
has gone up exponentially from 50 years
ago.
So I think if you talk about energy, we
really need to look at what are the real
issues are hurting us. Yes, the Iranians
using the Strait of Hormuz as a weapon
economically is hurting everybody across
the world, including working families in
our state and in our country. But if you
look long-term at energy policy, it's
been Democrat energy policy that has
made it more expensive on hardworking
people time and time again. As governor,
we want to look to alleviate those
policies as much as we can and then work
with our partners at the federal level
to drive costs down for the people of
our state and also the people of our
country.
>> We'll leave it there. I also want to say
thank you to your bus driver. Nice
smooth drive. I mean, there was
there wasn't too much swaying there. We
appreciate that. And you by the way have
a wonderful team because um in a word,
I'm relentless when it comes to trying
to get an interview and um they have
accepted um my constant texts, phone
calls, and emails and they've never
given me a hard time. So, I want to
thank them through you because you have
a nice team and a great bus driver.
>> Well, listen, I very much appreciate
that. Let's last thing I will say, thank
you for the time on your show. To the
people of Florida, we have a great
state. It didn't happen by accident.
Florida has had a consistent common
sense leadership for a long time and
that's why we're the best state in
America. That's why we're the state that
people run to, not run from. And if you
look at the states that people run from,
they're a lot of Democrat governors who
put in very stupid policies that
actually don't improve lives. So, I know
the election is right around the corner.
I'm asking for your vote this November
3rd.
>> And did you make that basket?
>> Oh, I did. I made it in two tries.
Don't doubt me. I can play.
>> All right. Thank you. And uh good luck
in a couple of days. And again, thank
you so much to you and your team. Uh be
well, be safe, and I know it's it's
relentless, but the finish line for both
you and and David Jolly is ahead and
we'll see who comes out on top. Thank
you, sir.
>> Thank you.
>> All right. Take care. God bless. Again,
Congressman Byron Donalds, thank you for
joining us and you can find our
conversations with both Donalds and
David Jolly at wftv.com. I'm Greg
Warmoth. Thank you for watching Central
Florida Spotlight and make sure and get
out to vote. We will have full coverage
on election night and reaction from all
the winners and those who fall short
again this coming Tuesday. Until then,
take care.
